title: The CORE-Well Model of primary school teachers’ occupational well-being as a multidimensional, relational, and process-oriented construct
abstract: Abstract Background Occupational well-being (OWB) is central to teachers’ professional functioning​ and relates to teacher retention, instructional quality, and student outcomes. Although teacher well-being research increasingly includes positive, engagement-related, and resource-oriented perspectives, many studies rely on predefined constructs, such as job satisfaction, stress, burnout, or emotion regulation. Less is known about how primary school teachers connect these dimensions in everyday professional practice. Aim This study examined how primary school teachers conceptualise OWB, which conditions they perceive as shaping it, and how they relate professional efficacy, recovery, and boundary-setting to their well-being. Method A theory-based qualitative exploratory study was embedded in an ongoing cross-sectional mixed-methods survey. The present paper draws on a defined data cut of N = 120 participants working in German primary school contexts; the qualitative model-building analysis ​included​ n = 51 cases and continue​ed until code saturation was reached. Open-ended responses were analysed using structured qualitative content analysis, combining deductive category development informed by ​Job Demands-Resources theoryand research on teacher well-being​ and resilience with inductive refinement. Results Teachers conceptualised OWB as multidimensional, comprising affective experiences, cognitive evaluations, and perceived meaning. They described OWB as shaped by job demands, contextual and relational resources, professional agency, and recovery-oriented regulation. Relational experiences with children, perceived pedagogical impact, and boundary management were particularly salient. Conclusion Primary school teachers’ OWB is best understood as dynamic, relational, and process-oriented. The findings specify how relational experiences, pedagogical responsibility, perceived impact on children’s learning and development, and boundary management are connected in primary school teachers’ OWB.
